description: Extracted color, type, component, and motion facts from Apple TV's iOS app for use as a build reference.

whatYouGet: Full true-black / single-accent color token table with hex values
SF Pro type scale from Large Title down to micro channel-tag labels
Primary/secondary/text button specs with padding, radius, and pressed states
Inset hero-card and continue-watching thumbnail component specs
Bottom tab bar and large-title navigation chrome specifications
Motion timing table distinguishing bespoke vs system-default transitions
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS product designer and SwiftUI engineer who has spent years building streaming and entertainment apps for Apple platforms, and who treats Apple's Human Interface Guidelines as the load-bearing spec rather than a suggestion. You default to system materials, system type, and the smallest possible set of custom colors, because that restraint is what makes an app feel native rather than bolted-on.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas & surfaces (dark, true-black product):
- Canvas: #000000 (pure OLED black — never a charcoal substitute)
- Surface 1 (cards/sheets): #1C1C1E, Surface 2 (elevated chips): #2C2C2E
- Divider/hairline: #38383A

Text ramp: primary #FFFFFF, secondary #98989F, tertiary #636366

Accent — exactly one: system blue #0A84FF (active tab tint, text links only), pressed #0060DF
Two deliberate exceptions to the "no second color" rule: a league pink #ED1A6F used ONLY on one
sports-subscription shelf/badge, and a live-sports red #FF453A used only for a pulsing LIVE dot.
Rating/gold accent: #FFD60A. Success: #30D158.

Type: SF Pro (Display for headings ≥20pt, Text below), Inter as the nearest free substitute.
Scale — Large Title 34pt/800, Hero 28pt/800, Row Header 22pt/700, Title3 20pt/600, Body 17pt/400,
Headline 15pt/600, Subhead 13pt/400, Caption 12pt/500, Eyebrow 11pt/700 (uppercase, +1.2pt track),
Button 15pt/600, micro channel-tag label 9pt/700. Tracking runs -0.8pt to -0.2pt on the two largest
sizes only; everything else sits at 0.

Buttons: primary CTA is solid white fill / black label, 12pt radius, 13pt vertical + 30pt horizontal
padding, pressed state #E5E5EA + scale 0.98. Secondary uses the system translucent fill
rgba(120,120,128,0.36) with an 8pt blur. Text links use the accent blue only, no underline.

Core card: a horizontal "continue watching" thumbnail at 16:9, ~196pt wide, 10pt radius, a 4pt-tall
resume-progress bar (white fill over a 28%-opacity white track) pinned to the bottom edge, and a
tiny top-left channel-source tag in a dark glass pill.

Hero pattern: the featured item is an INSET card (14pt horizontal margin, 16pt corner radius) rather
than full-bleed — the art appears to float rather than fill the screen — with a bottom scrim running
from transparent at 40% down to ~92% black at the base.

Radius scale: 6pt (tags/chips) → 10pt (cards) → 12pt (buttons/rows) → 16pt (hero/sheets) →
22pt (large modals) → full pill (segmented controls) → circle (avatars).

Chrome: bottom tab bar is a translucent material — blur(20px) saturate(180%) over ~92%-opaque black,
0.33pt top hairline, active glyph filled + tinted, inactive stroked + tertiary-gray, labels always
visible at 12pt/500.

Motion: press states settle in 120-150ms ease-out with a subtle scale (0.97-0.98); a live indicator
dot pulses opacity 1→0.4 on a slow ~1.2s loop; large-title collapse and sheet presentation both ride
the system's own transition curves rather than a custom one.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Treat pure black as sacred — if the canvas drifts toward any charcoal or near-black, OLED screens stop truly turning pixels off and the whole "floating art" illusion collapses.
2. Never let a second saturated hue creep into general chrome — the one accent blue exists so that "this is blue" always means "this is tappable," and diluting that removes the signal.
3. Make the hero card inset and rounded, not full-bleed — an edge-to-edge hero reads as a generic streaming billboard; the inset margin is what makes it feel authored rather than templated.
4. Keep the primary action white-on-dark rather than tinted, because a colored primary button would compete with the single accent color for the user's attention.
5. Reserve any brand-specific accent color (a league tint, a sponsor color, etc.) to exactly one clearly bounded surface — do not let it leak into shared chrome like tab bars or global buttons.
6. Default motion to system-provided curves and durations (spring physics, large-title collapse, sheet presentation) instead of hand-authored easing — bespoke motion reads as non-native on this platform.
7. Keep body copy at regular weight even when everything around it is heavy — restraint in the type scale is what separates an editorial-feeling surface from a shouting one.
8. Never crowd a row with badges beyond what's functionally necessary (a source tag, an occasional live indicator) — extra ornamentation on thumbnails undermines a deliberately quiet visual system.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / working title:
- Primary content type (film, TV, live sports, docs, mixed):
- Does the product have more than one accent color need (e.g. a live-sports tier, a sponsored channel)? If so, name them:
- Existing brand palette (if any) beyond the system accent:
- Target OS baseline (minimum iOS version) and whether tvOS parity matters:
- Key screens to design first (e.g. home, detail, player, search):
- Any existing component library or design tokens to reconcile against:
- Tone in one sentence (e.g. "quiet, editorial, gallery-like" vs "energetic, dense, broadcast"):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Palette definition — a token table (canvas, two surface steps, divider, three text tiers, the single accent + its pressed state, plus any bounded brand exceptions) with hex values and stated usage rules for each.
2. Type scale — a complete size/weight/line-height/tracking table from largest heading down to the smallest fixed label, annotated with which sizes should respect Dynamic Type and which must stay fixed.
3. Core component specs — primary button, secondary/glass button, text link, and the signature content-thumbnail component (aspect ratio, radius, progress-bar treatment, tag placement) each with exact padding, radius, and state values.
4. Hero/billboard treatment — full layout spec for the top-of-home featured item, including inset margins, scrim gradient stops, and the content hierarchy sitting on top of it.
5. Navigation chrome — bottom tab bar spec (height, background material, active/inactive treatment, label rules) and any large-title behavior.
6. Motion notes — a short table of the interactions that need bespoke timing (press feedback, pulsing indicators, transitions) versus those that should defer to system defaults.
7. Do/Don't list — five to eight concrete rules distilled from the choices above, phrased so a second designer joining later can self-check their work against it.
8. Open questions — anything in my answers above that's ambiguous or under-specified, flagged explicitly rather than silently assumed.
</what_to_give_me>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior mobile product designer who specializes in anime and fandom-driven streaming apps, fluent in translating a single confident accent color and heavy display type into a SwiftUI component library that still feels lightweight enough to ship.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas & surfaces (dark-only, no light mode shipped):
- Canvas: #000000 (true black, OLED)
- Surface 1 (sheets/trays): #16171A, Surface 2 (cards/pressed rows): #23252B, Surface 3 (tracks/chips): #2E3035
- Divider: #2A2C31

Text: primary #FFFFFF, secondary #A0A0A0, tertiary #6A6C70, on-scrim text #D8D8D8

Single interactive accent: brand orange #F47521 (pressed #D8610F, lighter tint #FF8C42) — used for
the primary CTA, active tab, a sliding segmented-control underline, and the resume-progress fill.
Secondary badge accents (never used as buttons): premium gold #FFC107 (ink text #1A1304), a
"simulcast" status green #2BB673, a "new episode" status blue #2A9DF4. Error red #E03E3E.

Type: a humanist sans with a distinctive heavy 900 "black" weight (Lato is the reference face; falls
back to SF Pro's heavy weight). Weights concentrate at 400/700/900 only.
Scale — Screen Title 32pt/900, Hero Title 28pt/900, Section Header 22pt/900, Row Header 18pt/700,
Body 16pt/400, Episode Title 15pt/700, Episode Synopsis 13pt/400, Meta Line 14pt/400,
Button Label 16pt/900 (+0.3pt tracking), Segmented Item 14pt/900, Badge 11pt/900 uppercase
(+0.4pt tracking), Tab Label 10pt/700, Caption 12pt/400.

Buttons: primary is a full-width 52pt pill-ish rectangle at 8pt radius, orange fill, white 900-weight
label with a leading play glyph; pressed state darkens to #D8610F + scale 0.98. Outline secondary
uses a 1.5pt semi-transparent white border on transparent fill.

Core card: hero art fills roughly 60% of screen height, full-bleed with no radius, under a bottom
scrim gradient (transparent → 55%-black at the midpoint → solid black at the base). Episode rows use
a 112x64pt thumbnail (6pt radius) with a small number chip top-left and a 3pt orange progress bar
pinned to the thumbnail's bottom edge.

A signature toggle control switches between two audio/subtitle tracks as a two-segment pill, inactive
segments outlined in translucent white, the active segment filled solid orange.

Radius scale: 4pt (badges/number chips) → 6pt (posters/thumbnails/toggle) → 8pt (buttons/search) →
12pt (sheets) → full pill (progress-bar end caps) → circle (avatars).

Depth: almost entirely flat — the scrim gradient IS the primary depth cue rather than drop shadows,
because shadows barely register on a true-black canvas. A floating CTA over key art gets a soft
0 4px 16px rgba(0,0,0,0.6) lift; bottom sheets get a deeper 0 -8px 32px shadow.

Motion: card press settles at scale 0.97 over ~150ms ease-out; a segmented-control underline slides
to its new position over ~220ms ease-out; transitioning into playback fades the current screen to
black over ~250ms before the player appears — a deliberate "lights down" beat, not an instant cut.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Let the one accent color do every job at once (CTA, active tab, underline, progress) rather than assigning different colors to different affordances — a single accent reads as more confident and is easier for users to learn.
2. Reserve any secondary status color strictly for informational badges, never for anything tappable — a badge-only color keeps the primary accent unambiguous as "the thing to press."
3. Default hero and detail imagery to the heaviest available type weight for titles, and keep everything else (body, synopsis) at the lightest weight in the scale — the contrast between heavy titles and light body text is what gives poster-style layouts their energy.
4. Use a gradient scrim, never a flat color panel, behind any text sitting on top of key art — a flat panel looks like a UI patch, a gradient looks like intentional cinematography.
5. Keep corner radii small and consistent across card types (thumbnails and posters share one radius, buttons share a slightly larger one) — inconsistent radii between similar components is one of the fastest ways a UI reads as unpolished.
6. Never let episode or continue-watching progress indicators disappear — a resumable-content signal is a core retention mechanic and should never be optional or hidden behind a tap.
7. Cap motion durations in the 150-300ms range and always ease-out on entry — content-dense, poster-forward UIs feel sluggish if transitions run any longer.
8. Avoid drop shadows as a primary depth technique on a true-black canvas — they're nearly invisible there, so lean on gradient scrims and flat surface-color steps instead.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / working title:
- Core content vertical (anime, general TV, gaming, other niche fandom):
- Primary accent color (hex) and whether it needs a "premium" or "new" secondary badge color:
- Does the content have multiple audio/language tracks that need a switcher control:
- Target device baseline (iPhone only, or iPad/tvOS parity too):
- Key screens to design first (browse grid, detail/hero, episode list, player):
- Existing typography license or brand font (if any) to substitute in:
- One sentence describing the emotional tone you want (e.g. "energetic and poster-like" vs "calm and editorial"):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color token table — canvas, three surface steps, three text tiers, the single interactive accent (plus pressed/tint variants), and any secondary badge-only colors, each with a stated usage boundary.
2. Type scale — full size/weight/line-height/tracking table, flagging which sizes use the heaviest weight and which stay at regular.
3. Button and toggle specs — primary CTA, outline secondary, and any two-way segmented toggle, each with exact padding, radius, and pressed-state values.
4. Signature card specs — the hero/key-art treatment (aspect ratio, scrim gradient stops) and the resumable-content row component (thumbnail size, progress-bar placement, number/status chip position).
5. Depth and elevation table — which surfaces get a shadow, which rely purely on the gradient scrim, and the exact shadow values for floating elements.
6. Motion notes — timing and easing for press states, control-toggle sliding, and any full-screen transition moment worth calling out.
7. Do/Don't list — five to eight rules a second designer could use to self-audit new screens against this system.
8. Flag any part of my project description above that's ambiguous rather than guessing silently.
</what_to_give_me>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS designer who specializes in premium, cinematic entertainment brands, skilled at translating a deep-navy 'theater' atmosphere and a glowing focus-state language into concrete SwiftUI tokens and components.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas & surfaces (dark-only, deep midnight-blue rather than black or gray):
- Canvas: #0A0E2A
- Surface 1 (cards/rows): #12152E, Surface 2 (sheets/search): #1A1F3D
- Divider: #2A3050

Text: primary #FFFFFF, secondary (cool periwinkle-gray) #A0A6C0, tertiary #5A6080

Accent pair: a primary brand blue #0063E5 (CTAs, primary buttons, progress fill) and a brighter
"glow" blue #1A75FF used exclusively for focus halos and selected-tile emphasis, pressed state
#0052BD. Semantic: live-event red #E5484D, new/premiere tag reuses the glow blue.

Type: an Avenir-family geometric humanist sans (Inter is the closest free substitute), weights
limited to 400/600/700 only — no thin or black weights anywhere.
Scale — Billboard fallback title 30pt/700, Detail Title 26pt/700, Section Header 20pt/700,
Row Header 18pt/700, Card Title 14pt/600, Synopsis 15pt/400, Metadata Strip 13pt/600 (+0.3pt
tracking), Subtitle 14pt/400, Meta/Count 12pt/400 tabular, Badge 10pt/700 uppercase (+1.0pt
tracking), Primary Button 16pt/700, Secondary Button 14pt/600, Tab Label 10pt/600.

Buttons: the primary CTA is unusual for the palette — a solid WHITE pill with a dark navy glyph and
label (not the brand blue), 48pt tall, 8pt radius, often with a soft blue glow sitting behind it.
Secondary actions use a translucent white glass fill (12% opacity) with a 1pt 24%-opacity white
border.

Signature navigation element: a row of landscape "portal" tiles (~160x96pt, 10pt radius) that each
gateway into a distinct sub-brand/universe, each rendered on its own tinted gradient with a centered
logo mark. Selecting or focusing any tile scales it to 1.04, adds a 2pt glow-blue border, and blooms
a soft blue shadow around it — this exact glow+scale treatment is reused for every focusable card in
the app, making it the system's unifying interaction language.

Content cards are always 16:9 landscape (never square or 1:1) at 220pt standard width, 6pt radius,
key art only with no title overlay by default. Continue-watching variants add a 3pt blue progress
bar at the bottom edge.

Hero treatment: a full-bleed billboard at ~62% of viewport height, a faint starfield of scattered
low-opacity white points behind the scrim, a vertical gradient from transparent to the canvas navy,
and — distinctively — the featured title's own logo ARTWORK centered low rather than a rendered text
title, with a muted auto-playing trailer cross-fading in after a few seconds of dwell time.

Radius scale: 6pt (content cards) → 8pt (buttons/chips/search) → 10pt (portal tiles) → 16pt (sheets)
→ circle (avatars/toggles).

Motion: the glow+scale focus transition runs ~180ms ease-out with no bounce; the hero's still-to-
trailer cross-fade takes ~600ms after a roughly 3-second dwell; button taps use a damped spring
(response ~0.25, damping ~0.8).
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Keep the canvas a rich navy rather than black or neutral gray — a true-black or gray canvas would read as a generic dark mode rather than a specific, ownable brand environment.
2. Split the accent into two roles — one blue strictly for actions (buttons, progress) and a brighter second blue strictly for focus/selection glow — conflating the two removes the visual distinction between "you can tap this" and "this is currently selected."
3. Make the primary CTA a bright, near-white pill rather than tinting it with the brand accent — over full-bleed key art, a white button reads more legibly and more cinematically than a colored one.
4. Apply the exact same glow+scale focus treatment to every focusable card type in the app (content tiles, portal tiles, anything selectable) — one unified interaction language is more recognizable than several similar-but-different ones.
5. Default to landscape 16:9 cards everywhere content is browsed — square tiles read as a music or podcast app, not a video streaming one, and consistency here matters more than any single screen's layout.
6. Prefer a title's own branded logo artwork over rendered text wherever the asset exists — logo art carries far more brand recognition than a generic type title ever will.
7. Keep type weights restricted to regular/semibold/bold only — introducing a thin or a black weight breaks the deliberately narrow, controlled type voice this system depends on.
8. Avoid neutral gray drop shadows as the main way of expressing elevation — let the scrim gradient and the blue focus glow do that work instead; gray shadows feel out of place against a navy environment.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / working title:
- Number of distinct sub-brands or content universes the app needs to gateway into (if any):
- Primary accent color (hex) and a secondary "glow/focus" tone if different:
- Do you have branded logo artwork per title, or will titles render as plain text:
- Target device baseline:
- Key screens to design first (home/billboard, portal/hub row, detail, browse grid):
- Existing type license or brand font to substitute in:
- One sentence on desired tone (e.g. "premium and aspirational" vs "playful"):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color token table — canvas, two surface steps, divider, three text tiers, the action-blue and the separate focus-glow blue with pressed/glow variants, plus any semantic colors (live, new).
2. Type scale — complete size/weight/line-height/tracking table restricted to the three allowed weights.
3. Button specs — the white primary pill and the glass secondary button, each with exact height, radius, padding, and glow treatment.
4. The unified focus/selection component — one reusable spec (scale factor, border width and color, glow radius, timing) that every focusable card type in the output should reference.
5. Hero/billboard spec — full layout including the starfield treatment, scrim gradient stops, logo-artwork placement, and the auto-trailer cross-fade timing.
6. Portal/hub row spec (if the project has sub-brands) — tile dimensions, radius, gradient-per-brand approach, and how it differs from a standard content card.
7. Motion notes — a short table covering focus transitions, hero cross-fade, and button press feedback.
8. Do/Don't list distilled into five to eight rules for a second designer to self-check against.
</what_to_give_me>

Heavy condensed type scale with a hard tabular-numerals requirement for all scores
Full game-card component spec (header, team rows, status pill, footer)

Live vs final status-pill states including exact pulse timing

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior mobile designer and SwiftUI engineer who has built live sports and scoreboard products, obsessive about tabular numerals, glanceable density, and the discipline needed to keep a single brand color legible across dozens of simultaneous live states.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas & surfaces (dark-first, deliberately NOT pure black so cards lift off it):
- Canvas: #0E0F11
- Surface 1 (card body): #18191B, Surface 2 (ticker chip/header): #212327, Surface 3 (pressed/final): #2B2D31
- Divider: #2A2C30

Text: primary #FFFFFF, secondary #9AA0A6, tertiary #6B7075

Brand accent: core red #D50A0A (logo block, active-tab indicator dot, section accents) plus a
brighter "action" red #CC0000 (CTAs, links, category tags), pressed #A50808. Two status colors that
are NOT the brand accent and must never be confused with it: live-game red #FF1A1A (with a pulsing
dot) and win-result green #1FAA59 (a finished game's winning score only). Rank/ranking gold #F2C200.
Error #E5484D (distinct from brand red).

Type: a bold condensed-leaning grotesque (Archivo is the reference face; SF Pro's heavy weight plus
forced tabular figures is the fallback), weights 400/700/800/900.
Scale — Screen Title 32pt/900, Headline 26pt/900, Section Header 22pt/800, Team Name 18pt/700,
Body 16pt/400, Story Title 15pt/700, large Score 26pt/900 (MUST be tabular), ticker Score 13pt/700
(MUST be tabular), Meta Line 14pt/400, Team Record 12pt/400, Button Label 16pt/800, Status Badge
11pt/900 uppercase (+0.5pt tracking), Category Tag 10pt/900 uppercase, Tab Label 10pt/700.

Non-negotiable rule: every score, clock, and ranking number renders with tabular (monospaced) figures
so digits never shift or misalign between cards — this is treated as a correctness requirement, not
a stylistic preference.

Buttons: primary CTA uses a tight 6pt corner radius (tighter than most consumer apps — deliberately
"sporty"), red fill, white 800-weight label with a leading play glyph, 14pt/28pt padding, pressed
#A50808 + scale 0.98.

Core card ("the atom"): a game-summary card with three stacked zones — a header strip naming the
league/series plus a live-or-final status indicator on the trailing edge; two team rows each pairing
a circular logo, team name, win-loss record, and a large tabular score (the winning/leading score in
white or, once final, green; the losing score dimmed to secondary gray); and a footer strip pairing
the live game clock with a "watch" link. A companion horizontally-scrolling ticker strip renders the
same information in a much more compact ~116pt-wide chip so an entire slate of live games can be
scanned in one glance near the top of the screen.

A live-status pill always uses the hot status-red fill with a small white dot that pulses opacity
between 1.0 and 0.4 on a ~1.2s loop; a finished game swaps the same pill to a muted gray "final"
treatment with the dot removed entirely — the color/dot pairing is the sole "this is happening right
now" signal in the whole system.

Radius scale: 3pt (status badges/tags) → 6pt (buttons/search) → 8pt (ticker chips/thumbnails) →
12pt (game cards) → 16pt (modals) → full pill (live/status pills).

Motion: the live-dot pulse loops continuously at ~1.2s ease-in-out; a changed score cross-fades with
a small ~1.06 scale "pop" over ~200ms; a tabbed underline slides to a new selection over ~200ms
ease-out; a card press settles at scale 0.98 over ~150ms.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Force tabular (monospaced) numerals on every score, clock, and ranking without exception — proportional digits shift column alignment as numbers update, which visibly breaks a scoreboard layout and must be treated as a bug, not a style choice.
2. Never let the "live" status color and the brand accent color be the same hue — using the brand red for both a logo/CTA and a live indicator would make it impossible to tell "this is our brand" apart from "this game is happening right now."
3. Reserve the win-result color exclusively for a finished game's winning score — using it anywhere else (as a general success color, say) breaks the one-glance "who won" readability this system is built around.
4. Keep the canvas a hair above true black rather than pure black — cards need enough contrast lift against the canvas to read as distinct layers without relying on borders.
5. Default to a dense, information-forward layout rather than a spacious editorial one — a scoreboard-style product succeeds by fitting more signal into one glance, so generous whitespace actively works against the product's purpose.
6. Mark the active tab or selection state with a small colored dot/indicator rather than a filled tint pill — a subtle indicator keeps icon colors legible while still clearly showing selection.
7. Use a noticeably tighter corner radius on buttons and cards than a typical consumer app (in the 6-12pt range rather than 16pt+) — tighter radii read as faster and more athletic, reinforcing a sports-broadcast feel.
8. Confine motion to the two places it earns its keep — the live pulse and a score-change "pop" — and keep everything else calm; overusing animation undermines the sense of density and speed the rest of the UI is built to project.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / working title:
- Primary content type (single sport, multi-sport scoreboard, general sports news, mixed):
- Brand accent color (hex) and whether it needs to be visually distinct from a "live now" status color:
- Does the product need a compact ticker/summary strip in addition to full detail cards:
- Target device baseline:
- Key screens to design first (scores feed, ticker, game/match detail, story feed):
- Existing type license or brand font to substitute in:
- One sentence on tone (e.g. "fast and information-dense" vs "calm editorial"):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color token table — canvas, three surface steps, divider, three text tiers, the brand accent (with its brighter action variant and pressed state), and the two status colors (live, win-result) called out as separate from the brand accent.
2. Type scale — full size/weight/line-height/tracking table, explicitly flagging every row that must use tabular figures.
3. The core "game card" component spec — header strip, team-row structure (logo/name/record/score), status-pill placement, and footer strip, with exact padding and radius.
4. The compact ticker-chip variant of the same component, sized for horizontal scanning.
5. Live-status pill spec — the pulsing live treatment and the muted "final" treatment, with exact timing for the pulse.
6. Button and navigation specs — primary CTA, tab bar treatment (dot indicator, not a tint pill), and a tabbed sub-navigation control if relevant.
7. Motion notes limited to the few moments that should animate (live pulse, score-change pop, tab-underline slide) with exact durations and easing.
8. Do/Don't list of five to eight rules, phrased so a second designer can self-audit a new screen against them before it ships.
</what_to_give_me>

name: Hulu Design System

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS designer specializing in dense, browse-heavy streaming catalogs, skilled at keeping a single electric accent color meaningful across a rail-stacked, content-forward SwiftUI layout.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas & surfaces (dark-only, warm-lifted so it never crushes artwork edges):
- Canvas: #0B0C0F (never pure #000000 — that's reserved for the video player)
- Deep black (player only): #000000
- Surface 1 (cards/sheets): #151619, Surface 2 (chips/modals): #1E2024, Surface 3 (pressed/divider): #2A2D33

Text: primary #FFFFFF, secondary #A0A4AB, tertiary #6B6F77

Single interactive accent: an electric green #1CE783 (pressed #15B869) used ONLY for the primary
"watch" verb, the active tab (icon AND label both turn green — unusually, green itself is the tab
indicator rather than a separate pill), the resume-progress fill, and toggle states. A live-content
red #F0476A exists purely as a status color for live/sports tiles and is never used for actions.

Type: a clean condensed grotesque (Graphik is the reference face, Inter the free substitute),
weights restricted to 400/600/800 only.
Scale — Details Hero Title 32pt/800, Screen Title 28pt/800, Rail Header 22pt/800,
Section Header 20pt/800, Episode Title 16pt/600, Tile Title 15pt/600, Body 15pt/400,
Metadata 13pt/400, Tile Subtitle 12pt/400, uppercase Label 11pt/800 (+0.6pt tracking),
primary Button 16pt/800, secondary Button 15pt/600, Tab Label 10pt/600, Badge 11pt/800.

Buttons: the primary "watch" CTA is unusual in that its label and icon render in near-black on top of
the bright green fill (not white) — this is a deliberate, tested contrast choice, not an oversight —
full-width, 52pt tall, 8pt radius, with a soft green glow shadow behind it. Secondary buttons use a
12%-opacity white glass fill at the same 8pt radius.

Core card: a 16:9 landscape tile (200pt standard, 260pt for a "spotlight" rail, 130pt-wide 2:3 poster
in movie-forward sections) at 6pt radius — deliberately NOT rounded further, to preserve the
rectangle's integrity. Continue-watching variants add a 4pt-tall green progress bar pinned to the
bottom edge over a 25%-opacity white track.

Distinctive navigation element: a horizontally-scrolling row of branded "hub" destination chips
(40pt tall, 8pt radius) sitting directly under the top nav, letting a user jump straight into a
partner or first-party content collection; entering a hub can re-skin its own rail headers with that
hub's accent while the green CTA color stays fixed platform-wide.

Radius scale: 0pt (full-bleed backdrops/video) → 6pt (content tiles/posters) → 8pt (buttons/chips/
search) → 12-16pt (sheets/modals) → full pill (filter chips, LIVE badge) → circle (avatars).

Depth: on this canvas, neutral gray shadows need to be unusually deep (40-50% opacity, 18-28pt blur)
to even register — so the signature elevation cue is chromatic instead: a soft green glow sits behind
the primary CTA and around any focused tile, doing the visual "lift" work that a gray shadow can't
achieve credibly on a dark surface.

Motion: tile press scales up slightly (1.0→1.04) over ~180ms ease-out with a focus shadow and green
ring fading in alongside a light haptic tap; the primary CTA itself springs to 0.97 scale on press
with a pulsing glow; rail scrolling uses native momentum with no snapping.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Use dark near-black rather than pure black for the general canvas, reserving true #000000 for the video player only — a lifted dark tone keeps poster-art edges from visually disappearing into the background.
2. Let the single accent color double as the CTA fill AND the active-tab indicator (icon and label both) rather than introducing a separate tint-pill mechanism — one color, one meaning, applied consistently everywhere it appears.
3. Pair the bright accent button with near-black label text rather than white — white-on-bright-green fails contrast testing more often than people expect, while a dark label passes comfortably and still reads as "the accent button."
4. Cap corner radius on content tiles at a conservative value (around 6pt) rather than rounding further — a landscape tile that's rounded too aggressively starts to look like a squared-off blob instead of a crisp rectangle.
5. Never hide or omit a resume/progress indicator on a partially-watched tile — for a catalog this dense, resume state is a primary navigation aid, not a decorative extra.
6. Keep rails/sections spaced generously apart vertically even though individual tiles sit close together horizontally — density inside a rail is good for scanning, density between rails makes the whole page feel cluttered.
7. Lean on a colored glow rather than a gray shadow for anything that needs to visually "lift" off the canvas — plain gray shadows need excessive opacity to register on a dark background and read as murky rather than crisp.
8. Restrict type weights to exactly three values (regular, semibold, extrabold) — adding a thin or medium weight dilutes the type voice this system depends on for quick scanning.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / working title:
- Primary content type (general TV/film catalog, live TV inclusion, branded partner hubs):
- Single interactive accent color (hex) and whether button label text should be dark-on-accent or white-on-accent:
- Do you need a "hub" or partner-destination navigation pattern:
- Target device baseline:
- Key screens to design first (home rails, details hero, hub row, episode list):
- Existing type license or brand font to substitute in:
- One sentence on tone (e.g. "dense and browse-heavy" vs "spacious and curated"):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color token table — canvas, deep-black (player-only), three surface steps, three text tiers, the single accent (with pressed state and a stated contrast rule for its label text), and any status-only colors (e.g. live).
2. Type scale — full size/weight/line-height/tracking table restricted to the three allowed weights.
3. Primary and secondary button specs, including the exact glow-shadow treatment behind the primary CTA.
4. Content-tile component spec — landscape/poster dimensions, radius, and the resume-progress-bar treatment for continue-watching variants.
5. Hub/destination-chip navigation spec, if relevant to the project, including how (or whether) it re-skins downstream rail headers.
6. Elevation notes — when to use a colored glow versus a neutral shadow, with exact values for each.
7. Motion notes for tile press, CTA press, and rail scroll behavior.
8. Do/Don't list of five to eight rules a second designer could use to self-check new screens against.
</what_to_give_me>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior mobile designer and SwiftUI engineer who has built live-streaming and chat-heavy community products, comfortable pushing a single loud accent color against strict monochrome chrome and designing a fast, role-colored chat system.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas & surfaces (dark-only, near-black on purpose so the accent doesn't visually vibrate):
- Canvas: #0E0E10 (never pure #000000 — true black makes the lime accent strobe)
- Surface 1 (cards/rows): #161618, Surface 2 (chat input/chips): #1F1F23, Surface 3 (menus/modals): #2A2A2E
- Divider: #2D2D31

Text: primary #FFFFFF, secondary #A6A6AD, tertiary #6E6E76, chat body #E4E4E9 (slightly softer than
pure white so role-colored usernames stand out against it), text-on-accent #0E0E10

Single brand/action accent: an electric lime-green #53FC18 (pressed #45D912, an alternate/legacy
tone #00E701) used for literally every primary action — follow/subscribe/go-live buttons, the active
tab, links, and a 2pt "online now" ring around a live streamer's avatar. It is a completely flat
fill with no glow or bloom — depth is never added to it.

The live/broadcasting indicator is ALWAYS a separate red (#FF1F44) and must never be rendered in the
accent green — conflating "live" with "brand action" would break the one thing viewers scan for.

Chat role-color system (a defining, non-negotiable part of the identity): moderator usernames render
in #3EA6FF with a matching badge chip, subscriber usernames in #FFC700 (badge chip shows the
subscription-month count), VIP in #FF4FD8, a founder/OG tier in the brand green #53FC18, a verified/
broadcaster tier in white-on-dark-chip, and ordinary users get a randomized color from a green-leaning
palette. Every colored username is preceded by a small role-badge chip — color alone is never the
sole signal.

Type: a tight modern grotesque (Inter is the reference face), weights 600-900 for anything
structural, 400 for message bodies.
Scale — Display 32pt/900, Screen Title 24pt/800, Section 20pt/800, Streamer Name 16pt/700,
Body 15pt/400, Card Title 13pt/700, Chat Username 13pt/700, Chat Message 13pt/400, Meta 13pt/400,
Button Label 15pt/800, Viewer Count 11pt/700 (tabular), Badge/LIVE 10pt/800 uppercase (+0.5pt
tracking), Tab Label 10pt/600.

Buttons run TIGHTER radii than most streaming apps — 6pt on primary buttons, not the 8-12pt common
elsewhere — reinforcing a rawer, less-corporate feel. Primary follow/go-live button: lime fill,
near-black label, 44-48pt tall. A "following" state swaps to a dark outline button rather than
staying green, so the accent is reserved for the action of following, not the state of already
following.

Signature screen structure: a stacked watch page — 16:9 video player on top (with a LIVE pill and a
translucent viewer-count chip), a compact "streamer bar" beneath it (avatar with the green online
ring, name plus a green verified check, category/viewer meta line, trailing follow button), and a
chat panel that consumes the rest of the vertical space and never has a fixed height.

Chat messages are deliberately dense — a ~9pt vertical gap between rows, 14pt horizontal padding —
because a fast live chat needs to show as many lines as possible; loosening that spacing would work
against the product's whole purpose. Inline custom emote sprites render at roughly 18x18pt with a
3pt radius.

Radius scale: 3pt (badge chips, emote sprites, live/viewer tags) → 6pt (buttons — notably tight) →
8pt (cards, thumbnails, chat input/send button) → 12pt (sheet top corners) → full pill (a "jump to
latest" pill) → circle (avatars, the online-ring, the live dot).

Motion: chat messages append with a small ~120ms fade plus a 4pt slide-up, auto-scrolling to the
newest message via a spring UNLESS the viewer has manually scrolled up; a follow action morphs its
label with a ~200ms cross-fade and a 1→1.06→1 scale bounce; the live pill's dot can pulse slowly
(opacity 0.6↔1.0 over ~1.5s).
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Never render the canvas as pure black — a true #000000 ground makes a saturated lime/green accent visually vibrate for many viewers, so a near-black canvas one step up is a legibility requirement, not a stylistic preference.
2. Keep the "live now" indicator strictly red, never the brand accent color — conflating "this stream is live" with "this is brand green" removes the one unambiguous signal viewers rely on while scanning a grid of channels.
3. Never color a chat username by role alone without an accompanying badge chip — color-only meaning fails for colorblind viewers, so the badge chip must always carry the same information redundantly.
4. Keep the brand accent as a completely flat fill with no glow, bloom, or gradient behind it — a neon-adjacent color needs to look confident and graphic, not soft or ambient.
5. Use noticeably tighter corner radii across buttons and cards than a typical consumer streaming app (6-8pt rather than 12-16pt) — tight radii are part of what makes this identity feel raw and unpolished-by-design rather than corporate.
6. Keep chat message spacing dense rather than roomy — a live chat's entire value proposition is showing as many recent messages as possible in limited vertical space, so generous padding actively works against the product.
7. Reserve the accent color for the ACT of following/subscribing, and switch to a neutral outline state once already followed — this keeps the accent meaningful as "you can still take an action here" rather than becoming pure decoration once every button is green.
8. Keep the video player as the largest single element on the watch screen at all times, with chat filling the remaining flexible space rather than a fixed height — burying the player behind a large chat panel undermines the core viewing experience.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / working title:
- Primary content type (general live-streaming, gaming-specific, a single creator's app):
- Brand accent color (hex) and whether it needs a distinct "live now" status color:
- Does chat need a role/tier system (moderator, subscriber, VIP, etc.) with badge chips:
- Target device baseline:
- Key screens to design first (watch page, browse/live grid, chat panel, follow/subscribe flow):
- Existing type license or brand font to substitute in:
- One sentence on tone (e.g. "raw and fast" vs "polished and premium"):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color token table — canvas, three surface steps, divider, four text tiers, the single accent (with pressed/alternate variants and a stated "text-on-accent" rule), the separate live-status red, and the full chat role-color table with matching badge-chip fills.
2. Type scale — full size/weight/line-height/tracking table, flagging which values must stay tabular (viewer counts, sub-month numbers).
3. Button specs — primary follow/action button (including its distinct "already following" state), tight radius values, and the chat-send button.
4. The stacked watch-page layout spec — video player overlay elements, streamer-bar component, and chat-panel structure with its flexible-height rule.
5. Chat message component spec — badge chip placement, role-color application, inline emote sizing, and the exact density (padding/gap) values.
6. Live-status and online-indicator specs — the LIVE pill treatment and the avatar online-ring, each with their pulse/animation timing.
7. Motion notes covering chat append/auto-scroll behavior, follow-button morph, and card press feedback.
8. Do/Don't list of five to eight rules a second designer could self-check new screens against, especially around color-only meaning in chat.
</what_to_give_me>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS designer specializing in prestige media brands, experienced at building a gradient-driven identity into disciplined SwiftUI tokens without letting the gradient sprawl beyond a tightly bounded set of brand moments.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas & surfaces (dark-only, the brand color IS the environment rather than a neutral gray/black):
- Canvas: #12053A (a deep saturated blue-violet, not a neutral dark)
- Deep black (player only): #000000
- Surface 1 (cards/sheets): #1B0B4D, Surface 2 (modals/chips): #250F5E, Surface 3 (pressed/divider): #36206E

Text: primary #FFFFFF, secondary (lavender-gray) #B0A8D0, tertiary #7E76A6

Accent is a GRADIENT, not a flat color: 135° sweep from electric blue #0046FF to violet #7B2FF7,
reserved strictly for the wordmark, the primary CTA, focus rings, and a "first-party original"
badge. A solid violet fallback #5A2BE0 (pressed #4A22BD) stands in wherever a true gradient can't
render cleanly — small toggles, a thin tab-bar underline indicator. A soft violet glow
(rgba(91,43,224,0.35)) sits behind the primary CTA and around focused tiles as the system's signature
elevation cue. Semantic: live-event gold #F2C94C, error #FF5C7A.

Type: a clean grotesque (Inter is the reference face), weights restricted to 400/600/800.
Scale — Billboard Title 32pt/800, Screen Title (Large) 28pt/800, Row Header 22pt/800,
Section Header 20pt/800, Episode Title 16pt/600, Tile Title 15pt/600, Body 15pt/400,
Metadata 13pt/400, Tile Subtitle 12pt/400, uppercase Label 11pt/800 (+0.6pt tracking),
primary Button 16pt/800, secondary Button 15pt/600, Tab Label 10pt/600, Badge 11pt/800.

Buttons: the primary "play" CTA fills its full width at 52pt tall, 8pt radius, with the true
diagonal gradient as its background and white label text — this is the ONE place white-on-gradient
is correct in the system. A slow ~4-second diagonal shimmer sweeps across it at idle to signal it as
the brand's primary action, and the violet glow sits behind it as a soft shadow. Secondary buttons
use a 14%-opacity white glass fill, no gradient.

Signature hero: a full-bleed AUTO-PLAYING MUTED TRAILER (not a static image) fills roughly 460pt at
the top of home, cross-fading to the next featured title's trailer roughly every 20 seconds with a
1.2-second dissolve — content and motion are fused into one continuous "marquee" moment rather than
a static billboard. A bottom-up gradient from transparent to the canvas purple anchors the overlaid
title/metadata/CTA row.

Content tiles run 200pt (16:9) or 130pt (2:3 poster) at a conservative 6pt radius; "first-party
original" content additionally carries a small gradient-BORDERED pill badge. On focus/press, any
tile scales to 1.04 and gains a 2pt gradient-colored ring plus the violet glow — echoing the same
focus language other prestige-tier apps use, but rendered in gradient rather than a flat color.

A launch-time profile gate presents a full-screen "who's watching" grid of large 96pt circular
avatars; the focused avatar gets a 2pt gradient ring.

Radius scale: 0pt (billboard/backdrop/video) → 6pt (content tiles) → 8pt (buttons/search/cards) →
12-16pt (sheets/modals) → full pill (filter chips, Originals badge) → circle (avatars, player
controls).

Motion: tile focus/press settles at scale 1.04 over ~180ms ease-out with the gradient ring and glow
fading in; the billboard trailer cross-fade runs 1.2s between titles on a ~20s cycle; the CTA's idle
shimmer loops continuously over ~4s; button press uses a damped spring (response ~0.25, damping ~0.7)
plus a darkening overlay rather than a simple color swap.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Treat the deep-purple canvas itself as brand identity rather than a neutral backdrop — stepping elevation toward gray instead of staying within the purple family would dilute the one thing that makes this environment instantly recognizable even on an empty screen.
2. Confine the gradient strictly to brand/action moments (wordmark, primary CTA, focus states, an "original content" badge) — applying it to body text, decorative panels, or anything non-interactive cheapens it from "marquee light" to generic ornamentation.
3. Always provide a solid-color fallback for any UI element small enough that a gradient can't render cleanly (thin indicators, tiny toggles) — a banded or muddy gradient at small sizes looks like a rendering bug, not a design choice.
4. Use white label text on the gradient CTA specifically — this is the one place in the system where white-on-accent is correct, precisely because the accent here is a full brand gradient rather than a single flat action color.
5. Keep the hero as a genuinely auto-playing, cross-fading trailer sequence rather than a static image with a play button — the moving marquee is the product's signature moment and a static hero would undersell the brand's prestige positioning.
6. Cap content-tile radius conservatively (around 6pt) even though the rest of the system uses generous radii elsewhere — an overly rounded tile competes with the artwork it's meant to frame.
7. Give rows and sections more vertical breathing room than a budget-tier streaming app would — generous spacing between content rows is itself a signal of premium positioning, independent of any color choice.
8. Reuse one consistent focus/selection treatment (scale + gradient ring + glow) across every focusable element — tiles, avatars, buttons — rather than inventing a new emphasis style per component.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
- App name / working title:
- Primary content type (prestige/original-heavy catalog, general streaming, live events):
- Brand gradient (two hex stops) and a solid fallback color for small UI:
- Does the product need a "first-party original" badge distinct from general content:
- Target device baseline:
- Key screens to design first (billboard/home, details, profile gate, browse grid):
- Existing type license or brand font to substitute in:
- One sentence on tone (e.g. "prestige and cinematic" vs "everyday and casual"):
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. Color token table — the brand-colored canvas, three surface steps within that same color family, three text tiers, the two-stop gradient plus its solid fallback and pressed state, the signature glow value, and any semantic colors (live, error).
2. Type scale — full size/weight/line-height/tracking table restricted to the three allowed weights.
3. Primary gradient-CTA spec (including the idle shimmer timing) and secondary glass-button spec.
4. Hero/billboard spec — the auto-playing trailer cross-fade cadence, scrim gradient, and the overlaid title/metadata/CTA layout.
5. Content-tile spec including the "original content" gradient-bordered badge and the unified focus/scale/glow treatment.
6. Profile-gate spec if relevant to the project (avatar size, grid layout, focus ring).
7. Motion notes covering tile focus, CTA shimmer, billboard cross-fade, and button press feedback with exact durations.
8. Do/Don't list of five to eight rules a second designer could self-check new screens against, especially around where the gradient is and isn't allowed to appear.
</what_to_give_me>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS designer who has spent years on large-catalog, poster-driven streaming products, disciplined about keeping a single saturated brand color rare and meaningful while the rest of the interface stays strictly monochrome.
</role>

<reference_data>
Canvas & surfaces (dark-only, warm charcoal rather than neutral gray or true black):
- Canvas: #141414 (a warm dark charcoal used everywhere except directly behind hero art, which drops to #000000)
- Surface 1 (cards): #1F1F1F, Surface 2 (sheets): #2A2A2A, Surface 3 (elevated menus): #3A3A3A
- Divider: #2B2B2B, dedicated input-field fill: #333333

Text: primary #FFFFFF, secondary #AAAAAA, tertiary #777777. Text on the brand-red button stays
white; text on a light/gray secondary button intentionally flips to black for contrast.

The brand accent appears in exactly three places and nowhere else: a red #E50914 (pressed #B7070F,
a dimmed #831010 for inactive states) used for the wordmark, the primary play button, and a
notification badge — never for links, borders, or general accents. A rotating set of saturated
profile-avatar colors (red, navy #3E3E91, mustard #F5D85C, forest green #4B8A3E, an orange
#F8981D reserved for a kids profile) exists ONLY on the profile-picker screen and must never bleed
into general app chrome. Notably, "success" and "downloaded" states use a neutral gray, not green —
green is deliberately avoided as a semantic color throughout.

Type: a proprietary humanist geometric sans (any clean grotesque with an SF Pro-style fallback
substitutes cleanly), weights restricted to 400/500/700.
Scale — Title-detail hero 32pt/700 (-0.4pt tracking, used only when no logo artwork exists),
Section/Row Header 17pt/700, Screen Title 20pt/700, Episode Title 17pt/500, Body 14pt/400,
Metadata 13pt/400, secondary Metadata 12pt/400, primary Button 17pt/700, secondary Button 15pt/500,
Badge 11pt/700 uppercase (+0.4pt tracking), Tab Label 10pt/500, Rating/Cert chip 12pt/700.

Buttons: the primary play control uses a corner radius of just 4pt — soft but distinctly NOT a full
pill, which is treated as a signature detail rather than an oversight — red fill, white 700-weight
label with a leading play glyph, full width, 48pt tall. Secondary actions (add-to-list, info, share)
use a 15%-opacity white glass fill or solid dark-gray fill at the same 4pt radius, never a pill.

Core card ("the atomic unit"): a 2:3 PORTRAIT poster tile — deliberately not landscape — at the same
signature 4pt radius, no border, no shadow, sitting flat on the canvas; only surface-color contrast
separates it from its background. A resumable title's tile carries a thin 2pt red progress bar
pinned to the very bottom edge.

Hero treatment: a full-bleed landscape image or auto-playing muted trailer bleeds to the screen
edges at the top of the browse feed, with NO app header of any kind above it except the small red
wordmark image — no search bar, no title text, no profile icon at this position, because the brand
treats the wordmark alone as sufficient identification. A vertical gradient over the lower 40% of the
hero fades it into the canvas color, and the featured title's own logo artwork (an image, not
rendered type) sits at roughly 60-65% width on top of that gradient.

A signature ranked-list row renders a set of giant outlined ordinal numerals (roughly 160pt tall,
colored to match the canvas so they read as a subtle debossed shape) directly behind each poster in
sequence, with each poster overlapping and partially covering its numeral's inner edge — an
instantly recognizable, hard-to-mistake-for-anyone-else's layout.

Radius scale: 0pt (hero/backdrop images) → 4pt (the signature radius — posters, buttons, inputs,
secondary buttons) → 8pt (a download progress ring) → 12pt (square game tiles, sheets) → full pill
(category filter chips) → circle (avatars).

Depth: almost entirely flat by design — posters and tiles carry no shadow at all, and the canvas's
own contrast against surface-color steps does essentially all of the separation work. The one
"lift" moment in the whole system is the hero's gradient fade, which is explicitly a color
transition rather than a drop shadow.

Motion: tapping a poster triggers a shared-element transition of the poster image into the detail
screen's hero position over roughly 350ms with a damped spring; the hero cross-fades from a static
key-art image to a muted auto-playing trailer after a short idle delay (a couple of seconds);
an add-to-list control rotates its icon and cross-fades between a plus and a checkmark glyph over
about 200ms; most other interactions use 250-400ms springs and nothing runs faster or louder than
that.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Restrict the single brand-red accent to exactly three roles — the wordmark, the primary play action, and a notification badge — and never let it appear as a border, a link color, or general decoration; scarcity is what keeps it meaningful.
2. Default every content tile to a 2:3 portrait aspect ratio, never landscape — a portrait poster grid is the entire visual identity of a large, browse-first catalog, and switching to landscape tiles undermines that instantly.
3. Use a warm dark charcoal for the general canvas rather than a neutral gray or true black, reserving pure black specifically for the area directly behind hero artwork — the warmth keeps the UI from feeling cold or generic.
4. Never use green as a semantic "success" or "downloaded" color — pick a neutral gray instead, keeping green entirely out of the palette so it can't be confused with any other product's conventions.
5. Keep the header above the main content feed reduced to a single wordmark image with no accompanying search bar, title text, or icon — the confidence of "you already know what this app is" is itself part of the brand voice.
6. Standardize on a small, distinctly-not-a-pill corner radius (around 4pt) across posters, buttons, and inputs — a consistent, deliberately modest radius is a recognizable signature that a fuller pill shape would erase.
7. Keep poster tiles completely flat — no border, no shadow — and rely purely on surface-color contrast against the canvas for separation; adding shadow to every tile in a dense grid creates visual noise at scale.
8. Confine any profile-specific or seasonal accent colors strictly to the profile-picker screen — they must never leak into shared browse, detail, or player chrome.
</house_rules>
